title: MCPs and KDEs in R: Old Skool Analyses
text:
This section contains explanations and guiding resources, but no code, since I haven’t used these methods in R in a long time. You can also perform both of these methods in QGIS, and probably ArcGIS too.

Key resources
If you want some R code, consider using the amt (animal movement tools) R package, and refer to this publication: Signer & Fieberd, 2021: A fresh look at an old concept: home-range estimation in a tidy world https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8048401/
This publication also makes a great point: since there area many ways to define a home range, make sure you start your research with a good question! Only then will you be prepared to know which statistical methods can actually help you answer your questions.
Fieberg & Börger, 2012: Could you please phrase “home range” as a question?


Minimum Convex Polygons (MCPs)
Minimum Convex Polygons (MCPs) are the oldest method used to estimate an animal’s home range. Given a set of locations from an animal’s tracking data, you simply draw a shape around the outermost points, so all points are either inside or form the edge of the polygon. Some studies these days still use them as a method of home range estimation so that they can be compared with past methods, or because they are quick, simple and intuitive. Sometimes, that’s what your stakeholders might want, or if you are just getting started in movement ecology, it is a great first step to learn.
One use of MCPs that I saw during my time as a wildlife conservation research consultant in Taiwan was rolling MCPs e.g. seeing how the size of a 10-day MCP changes over time. When an animal is newly released in an area (in our case, rescued/rehabilitated Formosan black bears), seeing how the size of it’s average 10-day (or whatever timeframe you want) home range changes over time is a nice way to visualise post-release exploration and home range stabilisation, or identify other significant life events like hibernation.


Kernel Density Estimates (KDEs)
Kernel Density Estimates (KDEs) were the next step in the evolution of home range estimation. They work by considering the DENSITY of GPS points, not just where they are located in space. If there is an area where you have more locations from your tracked animal, it would be This is where you may encounter terms like the “50% home range” - the most heavily used area where the animal spends half of it’s time/locations. Similarly, a 95% home range would contain the 95% of points used most, omitting the 5% outermost/outlying points.
The biggest weakness of the traditional KDE is that it takes into account space, but not time. In other words, KDEs assume your tracking data is IID - Independently and Identically Distributed. This basically means that there should be no temporal autocorrelation between GPS points. For VHF tracking datasets, or GPS datasets with a very low fixing frequency, this assumption may hold. However, many modern datasets sample locations at a rate that means they are autocorrelated in space and time. This is why, especially before more modern methods were developed, many research workflows would want a standardised GPS sampling schedule, forcing you to clip out a lot of your hard-earned locations from modern datasets. A standardised sampling schedule might be fine for a researcher’s specially-designed project, but not for real-life wildlife managers. Many modern GPS datasets contain locations separated by only a few hours, or even a few minutes, and sometimes in specific circumstances only.
For example, when we released black bears back into the wild, we would have their GPS collars set to record locations every 10 minutes for the first few days, so we can react if something goes wrong post-release. Then, we would set it to record every hour, and eventually every 2 hours, to optimise the battery life of the tracker so we can track the bear for as long as possible. However, if the collared bear then approached a village, crossing a digital fence we have set on the GPS collar software, the collar would start uploading locations at a higher frequency again, so we can track the bear at a higher resolution and try drive it away from town to avoid a conflict situation developing.
In another example, Druid Technology tags can use a BOOST mode to record high-frequency locations when they detect a sudden increase in ODBA (Overall Body Dynamic Acceleration) - e.g. when a bird starts flying. This allows you to capture more of the bird’s flight path in extreme detail. In cases like these with variable fix rates, KDEs can produce some pretty whacky shapes that are not reliable home range estimates.
This is a key limitation that has since been addressed (see ctmm chapter of this guide).
If you want to run KDEs, you can set your data as IID in ctmm, and the akde() function will run a traditional KDE.

title: move2 package: Net-Squared Displacement & more
text:
Net-Squared Displacement
Now we’ve done some more basic analyses, it’s time to level up. When studying animal movement, net-squared displacement (NSD) is sometimes pretty useful. This is especially so when we want to learn about an animal’s relationship to the places it inhabits, or at least a given point.
NSD simply measures the distance (or “displacement”) from a given point (normally the first point in the dataset analysed). From this, we can answer the following questions - What movement mode does the animal show? Does it migrate, have a set home range, or is it nomadic? - Has the animal settled into a set home range? - Is the animal exploring new areas further from home/the release point? When? How long?
These are especially pertinent questions when dealing with animal translocations or reintroductions, and/or when studying migratory animals.
Don’t just think about this in a 2D sense, think about altitude as well. An animal might move seasonally up to higher altitudes, which aligns well with the ways of interpreting NSD curves to determine movement modes.


The move2 package
An easy way to calculate NSD is offered by the move2 package. Building upon the popularity and success of the original move package, this is a great resource. Check out the move2 vignettes and website to learn about what it can do!
First thing’s first, we need to convert our data from a tibble or dataframe into a move2 object

# convert data to move2 object
duck1_y2_mv <- mt_as_move2(
  duck1_y2,
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
  time_column = "time",
  track_id_column = "id"
)

# inspect move2 object
duck1_y2_mv

# A <move2> with `track_id_column` "UUID" and `time_column` "time"
# Containing 1 track lasting 365 days in a
# Simple feature collection with 5668 features and 18 fields
# Geometry type: POINT
# Dimension:     XY
# Bounding box:  xmin: 144.4083 ymin: -38.26497 xmax: 144.5623 ymax: -38.1992
# CRS:           NA
# # A tibble: 5,668 × 19
#    UUID   time                     t altitude altitude_ellipsoid speed
#  * <chr>  <dttm>               <dbl>    <dbl>              <dbl> <dbl>
#  1 c4c9a… 2021-01-20 14:58:49 1.61e9      2.1               -1.6   0.3
#  2 c4c9a… 2021-01-20 15:58:16 1.61e9     11.3                7.6   0
#  3 c4c9a… 2021-01-20 17:58:49 1.61e9      0.6               -3.1   0.9
#  4 c4c9a… 2021-01-20 18:59:09 1.61e9    103.                99.2   0
#  5 c4c9a… 2021-01-20 19:58:10 1.61e9     17.1               13.4   0.3
#  6 c4c9a… 2021-01-20 20:58:38 1.61e9     48.6               44.9   0.1
#  7 c4c9a… 2021-01-20 21:58:30 1.61e9     54.7               51     0.1
#  8 c4c9a… 2021-01-20 22:58:31 1.61e9     85                 81.3   0.6
#  9 c4c9a… 2021-01-20 23:59:16 1.61e9     76.9               73.2   0.1
# 10 c4c9a… 2021-01-21 00:58:43 1.61e9     56.1               52.4   0
# # ℹ 5,658 more rows
# # ℹ 13 more variables: north_speed <dbl>, east_speed <dbl>,
# #   course <dbl>, satellite_used <dbl>, positioning_mode <dbl>,
# #   hor_accuracy <dbl>, ver_accuracy <dbl>,
# #   gps_time_consumption <dbl>, data_source <chr>, hdop <dbl>,
# #   vdop <dbl>, distance <dbl>, geometry <POINT>
# # ℹ Use `print(n = ...)` to see more rows
# Track features:
#           UUID
# 1 c4c9ad1ddc4e



Data preparation and checks in move2
We can also do some other checks on the data. For example, we can check the Coordinate Reference System (CRS), which all geospatial data should be assigned.
In case you hadn’t already ordered your tracking data temporally, you can check that using mt_is_time_ordered(). You can also ensure any duplicated rows are removed. We don’t want them messing up our analyses!

# check our CRS
sf::st_crs(duck1_y2_mv)
# currently NA
# provide an appropriate CRS for our data - EPSG:4326
sf::st_crs(duck1_y2_mv) <- 4326

# check the data is ordered by time
assertthat::assert_that(mt_is_time_ordered(duck1_y2_mv))
# check there are no duplicate rows
duck1_y2_mv <- mt_filter_unique(duck1_y2_mv)



(Net-Squared) Displacement
The time has come to make our net-squared displacement columns. I just copied the code provided on the move2 vignettes. Again, check them out!
First we will make a displacement column, then we square it. The reason for squaring displacement is basically since it becomes easier to spot changes in the data.

# create a displacement column
duck1_y2_mv <- duck1_y2_mv %>%
  mutate(
    displacement = c(sf::st_distance(
      !!!syms(attr(., "sf_column")),
      (!!!syms(attr(., "sf_column")))[row_number() == 1]
    ))
  )

# now make net squared displacement (square displacement)
duck1_y2_mv <- duck1_y2_mv %>%
  mutate(nsd = displacement^2)

# summary stats (in km - divided by 1000)
# displacement - km
summary(duck1_y2_mv$displacement) / 1000
#  Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
# 0.000   1.468   3.577   3.212   3.708   7.507

# nsd - km2
summary(duck1_y2_mv$nsd) / 1000000
#  Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
#   0.000   2.155  12.793  13.144  13.748  56.350



Plotting NSD in ggplot
Of course, no good analysis would be complete without a plot. That’s the power of NSD.
We can use a classic ggplot, like below.

# plot nsd over time using ggplot
duck1_y2_mv %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(
    x = time,
    y = as.numeric(units::set_units(nsd, "km2"))
  )) +
  ylab("Distance from start point (km2)") +
  ggtitle("Duck 1 Year 2 Net Squared Displacement") +
  theme_bw()



Plotting NSD using dygraphs
However! We can also consider using the dygraphs package, which is especially awesome for long time-series datasets where we might want to zoom in and out on different sections of the data.
To use the dygraphs package, we need to turn our data into a timeseries using the xts package. However, xts won’t accept a move2 object; the workaround is to extract the nsd column from our move2 object and stick it back onto our original tracking tibble. Since move2 uses the units package, our nsd column in the move2 object is a “units” object, so we also convert it to a plain ol’ numeric data type so we can successfully stick it onto our tibble. We will also divide nsd by 1,000,000 so it is represented in km2, not m2.

duck1_y2 <- duck1_y2 %>%
  mutate(nsd = as.numeric(duck1_y2_mv$nsd) / 1000000) # convert from m2 to km2

# now we can make the dygraph
(duck1_y2_nsd_dygraph <- duck1_y2 %>%
  select(time, nsd) %>%
  xts::xts(x = .$nsd, order.by = .$time) %>%
  dygraphs::dygraph() %>%
  dygraphs::dyAxis("y", label = "Distance from start point (km2)") %>%
  dygraphs::dyOptions(colors = "blue") %>%
  dygraphs::dyRangeSelector())

title: Loading and Processing GPS data
text:
Introduction
This tutorial introduces how to load and process GPS tracking data in R.


Data background:
We have data from 3 Pacific Black Ducks from Dr Hui Yu’s PhD project.
For your own purpose, you may want to load in your own GPS data. Otherwise, you can download some from Movebank - a free, online animal tracking database (https://www.movebank.org/cms/movebank-main)
Here we will just focus on loading the data of one of the ducks.
We will then use glimpse() to check the first few rows of each column of the data to understand what we are working with and how to process it for our analyses.


Import data

duck1 <- read_csv(
  "00_raw_data/Ecotopia-Data-[20200101-20260504]/c4c9ad1ddc4e[5210]-LocationData-GNSS-[20200101-20260504].csv"
)
duck2 <- read_csv(
  "00_raw_data/Ecotopia-Data-[20200101-20260504]/ea14dcaf2d4b[5246]-LocationData-GNSS-[20200101-20260504].csv"
)

duck3 <- read_csv(
  "00_raw_data/Ecotopia-Data-[20200101-20260504]/f914c5bac5d0[5239]-LocationData-GNSS-[20200101-20260504].csv"
)



Checking data
There are many ways to check your data in R. You could use the head() and tail() functions, str(), print(), View() or glimpse(). I personally like glimpse() as it shows the first few rows of each column, unlike head() or tail().

# check data
glimpse(duck1)

# Rows: 34,429
# Columns: 20
# $ UUID                   <chr> "c4c9ad1ddc4e", …
# $ `Transmitting time`    <dttm> 2020-01-19 08:1…
# $ `Collecting time`      <dttm> 2020-01-19 08:1…
# $ Longitude              <dbl> 200.0000, 200.00…
# $ Latitude               <dbl> 200.00000, 200.0…
# $ Altitude               <dbl> 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 6…

# ... etc



Processing data
Druid tags set latitude and longitude as 200 if the fix failed. We will flag these as “Failed” and the rest as “Successful” in a new column called “fix_success” We will also flag fixes where Altitude < 0 as “Failed” as well, as these are likely to be errors We will also rename the columns so they are easier to refer to, make a new numeric timestamp column, ensure data arranged by chronological order, and select the columns we want in a specified order.
While here we are doing this just for duck1, ideally we would make a function to do this for all our tracking datasets - especially if they come in the same data format.

duck1 <- duck1 %>%
  mutate(
    fix_success = ifelse(
      Latitude == 200 & Longitude == 200 | Altitude < 0,
      "Failed",
      "Successful"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(fix_success == "Successful") %>%
  rename(
    id = UUID,
    transmitting_time = `Transmitting time`,
    time = `Collecting time`,
    longitude = Longitude,
    latitude = Latitude,
    altitude = Altitude,
    altitude_ellipsoid = `Altitude (Ellipsoid)`,
    speed = Speed,
    north_speed = `North Speed`,
    east_speed = `East Speed`,
    down_speed = `Down Speed`,
    course = Course,
    satellite_used = `Satellite used`,
    positioning_mode = `Positioning mode`,
    hor_accuracy = HorAccuracy,
    ver_accuracy = VerAccuracy,
    gps_time_consumption = `GPS time consumption`,
    data_source = `Data Source`,
    hdop = HDOP,
    vdop = VDOP
  ) %>%
  # make a new column called t which is time in UNIX timestamp format
  mutate(t = as.numeric(time)) %>%
  arrange(time) %>%
  select(
    id,
    time,
    t,
    longitude,
    latitude,
    altitude,
    altitude_ellipsoid,
    speed,
    north_speed,
    east_speed,
    course,
    satellite_used,
    positioning_mode,
    hor_accuracy,
    ver_accuracy,
    gps_time_consumption,
    data_source,
    hdop,
    vdop
  )

We will also cut the dataset into separate years. For the rest of this tutorial, we are focusing on the 2nd year of duck movement data.

# cut dataset so it is just the first year of the duck movement
duck1_y1 <- duck1 %>%
  filter(time < as.POSIXct("2021-01-21"))

# filter for duck1 to second year of movement data
duck1_y2 <- duck1 %>%
  filter(time >= as.POSIXct("2021-01-21") & time < as.POSIXct("2022-01-21"))



Filtering data
We can calculate the step lengths between points and figure out if there are any suspicious outliers This should be combined with visual inspection of the map & data (often easier in QGIS etc)

# calculate time and distance of each step
timeDiff = diff(as.numeric(duck1_y2.df$time) / 3600) # in hours
distDiff = sqrt(diff(duck1_y2.df$X)^2 + diff(duck1_y2.df$Y)^2)

sum(timeDiff > 1) / length(timeDiff)
# 0.5088308

# make a histogram
hist(
  distDiff,
  breaks = 30,
  xlab = "Step Length",
  main = "Duck 1 year 2 Step Length - frequency",
  col = "gray70"
)
# We can see there's probably an outlier since our line goes all the way to 10,000.

title: Movement Ecology Toolbox
text:
Movement ecology is a constantly-evolving discipline. Especially in the past decade, there have been a lot of new advances and tools coming out. It can thus be hard to synthesise and learn about all the different analytical options available to us, and it can feel really confusing and overwhelming sometimes!
In this tutorial series, I share the tools, packages and workflows I have personally used in my job as a wildlife conservation research consultant, and in my postgraduate studies at both the University of Oxford (MSc) and Deakin University (PhD). As I continue to use learn and use more tools myself, I will update this website.
I hope it gives you some more confidence and clarity in how to analyse your animal tracking data :)
If you have queries or questions, please contact me at j.bolam@deakin.edu.au
This is a Quarto website. To learn more about Quarto websites visit https://quarto.org/docs/websites.

title: home range, occurrence distributions, periodicity & more using continous-time movement models
text:
ctmm (continous time movement models) is a very powerful package that deals with a key problem in modern tracking data; autocorrelation.
As tracking technology improves, it is more feasible to get finer-scale data, with less time between location fixes. This means that in most modern datasets, we have pretty detailed data on animal movements.
Location x will thus be inherently closer in space and time to location x-1, compared with location x-100. If we were only taking one location per week, this assumption may not hold as much. This greatly impacts what kind of analyses we can do. Previous home range calculation methods like kernel density estimates (KDE) look solely at the density of fixes in a location; the denser they are, the more important that area is supposed to be, and the more ‘core’ that area is in the animal’s home range.
However, what happens when your fixing interval changes? Sometimes you might take locations every 1 minute, then 10 minutes, then every 1h, then only twice a day. This depends on your management goals and what you what to use your battery life on.
In the past, movement ecologists often thinned their data so the assumptions of the analytical methods can hold true. This is stupid. Why should we have to get rid of our hard-earned data? We should instead be making better analytical tools.
In the past, discrete-time correlated random walk models (CRW) served as the foundation for analysing location data. However, they confound the sampling and movement processes, thus their parameters depend sensitively on the sampling schedule, meaning it is difficult to draw inferences on the underlying movement processes. The animals keep moving even when they are not being sampled, of course.
ctmmm treats animal movement data as a continuous, not discrete, process. It fits your data to a variety of different movement models, to find the optimal assumption.

IID: independent identical distribution - no autocorrelation in the data.
BM (Brownian Motion): treats animal movement as particles - a standard model of regular diffusion, where velocities are uncorrelated and space use is not limited. BM can be appropriate for data that are sampled both too coarsley to reveal velocity autocorrelation, and too briefly to show range residency. Not suitable for Home Range analses as it is by design an endlessly diffusing process.
OU: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck - combines brownian motion with a tendency to stay in a given area. Used where data lacks evidence of directional persistence.
IOU: Integrated Ornstein Uhlenbeck. Diffuses endlessly like BM, but unlike BM, features autocorrelated velocities at short time scales. IOU is therefore appropriate for finely sampled data sets that show directional persistence, but where sampling duration was too brief to identify range residency.
OUF - Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Foraging - a hybrid of the OU and IOU processes that features both correlated velocities and restricted space use (Fleming et al. 2014a,b). The OUF process will be appropriate for many modern data sets where sampling is both fine enough to reveal velocity autocorrelation and long enough to show range residency.

Read up on the different movement models ctmm offers (Calabrese et al,. 2016), so you understand how your data is interpreted and what you can and can’t do with it.


Here’s a link to the ctmm website - they have a few great vignettes https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/
ctmm is constantly being updated and has a very active google user’s group. Check it out if you need help. https://groups.google.com/g/ctmm-user?pli=1

title: Easy tracking analyses in R
text:
Once we’ve loaded and plotted our data, it’s time to do some basic analyses.

Altitude over time
Nothing too fancy, just things like plotting the altitude of our tracked animal over time. Let’s get into it!
There are two options to plot up your data. One is a good ole-fashioned ggplot. If you want a static map, that’s fine. The other option is a dygraph, which is an interactive plot. Dygraphs are perfect for long time-series data and data exploration, where you want to zoom in and out and inspect every nook and cranny of your dataset.

# altitude over time - in a dygraph format
(duck1_y2_altitude_dygraph <- duck1_y2 %>%
  select(time, altitude) %>%
  xts::xts(order.by = .$time) %>%
  dygraphs::dygraph() %>%
  dygraphs::dyAxis("y", label = "Altitude (m)") %>%
  dygraphs::dyOptions(colors = "grey") %>%
  dygraphs::dyRangeSelector())

# altitude over time - ggplot
(duck1_y2_altitude_plot <- ggplot(duck1_y2, aes(x = time, y = altitude)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Duck 1 Year 2 Altitude Over Time") +
  xlab("Time") +
  ylab("Altitude (m)") +
  theme_minimal())

From these graphs, you might see clear anomalous points that were missed in our previous filtering. E.g., we might want to remove points over 5000m or 10,000m

# we can see some points where the altitude is super high - over 5000m or even 10,000m.
# this is probably an error, so we will filter out any points over 5000m
duck1_y2 <- duck1_y2 %>%
  filter(altitude < 1000)

# then you can re-run the plots above and save them if you want

# save plot
ggsave(
  filename = "03_plots/duck1_altitude.png",
  plot = duck1_altitude_plot,
  width = 8,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)



Distance and time between points
We might also want to calculate the distance and time between subsequent GPS fixes. Here’s the code to do it by calculating the mean and cumulative distances between points.

# mean distance between points - distHaversine from geosphere package
duck1_y2 <- duck1_y2 %>%
  mutate(
    distance = distHaversine(
      cbind(longitude, latitude), # find the Haversine distance between a given lat lon point
      lag(cbind(longitude, latitude)) # and the previous lat lon point (lag function shifts data back 1)
    )
  )

# check it worked
glimpse(duck1_y2)

summary(duck1_y2$distance)
#  Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max.     NA's
#   0.00    10.34    23.11   181.32    63.81 10626.82        1

hist(
  duck1_y2$distance,
  breaks = 20,
  main = "Histogram of distances between points",
  xlab = "Distance (m)"
)

# calculate cumulative distance between each point and previous point
# it needs to account for the NA in the first row
duck1_y2 <- duck1_y2 %>%
  mutate(cumulative_distance = cumsum(replace_na(distance, 0)))
# find total cumulative distance by calling the final row
duck1_y2$cumulative_distance[nrow(duck1_y2)]
# 998852.6 m
998852.6 / 1000
# 998.8526 km

Another option is to calculate the length of the straight-line distance between our GPS points.

# figuring out the length of the straight-line distance between points
# (has it's issues if you have big time gaps between fixes)
# Create an sf POINT object from the GPS points (assuming WGS84)
duck1_y2_points <- st_as_sf(
  duck1_y2,
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
  crs = 4326 # WGS84
)

# Example: Transform to CRS 7855 (Australia)
duck1_y2_GPS_points_7855 <- st_transform(duck1_y2_points, crs = 7855)

# Combine the points into a LINESTRING
duck1_y2_line_7855 <- duck1_y2_GPS_points_7855 %>%
  summarise(geometry = st_combine(geometry)) %>% # Combine all points into one multilinestring
  st_cast("LINESTRING") # Cast to LINESTRING

plot(duck1_y2_line_7855)

# Save to shapefile
st_write(
  duck1_y2_line_7855,
  "01_tidy_data/duck1_y2_movement_path.shp",
  delete_layer = TRUE
)

# save as RData with duck1_y2_GPS_points_7855

save(
  duck1_y2_GPS_points_7855,
  duck1_y2_line_7855,
  file = '01_tidy_data/duck1_y2_GPS_points_line_sf_7855.RData'
)
# reload sf version of duck1_y2 GPS points in 7855 projection with a line shapefile too
load('01_tidy_data/duck1_y2_GPS_points_line_sf_7855.RData')

# Calculate total movement path length (planar, no terrain)
# This is an ESTIMATE based on the length of the lines between the GPS data.
# In reality, the distance will be even larger, although we cannot say by how much.
st_length(duck1_y2_line_7855)
# 986873.7 [m]
# in km
st_length(duck1_y2_line_7855) / 1000
# 986.8737 km
# pretty similar to the method above with cumulative distance between points

Finally, here’s some code to calculate the time lag in minutes and hours between each GPS point.

# calculate time lag in mins and hours between each gps point
duck1_y2 <- duck1_y2 %>%
  mutate(
    time_diff_h = as.numeric(difftime(time, lag(time), units = "hours")),
    time_diff_m = as.numeric(difftime(time, lag(time), units = "mins"))
  )
# check it worked
glimpse(duck1_y2)
# success

Well done!

title: Making and animating maps in R
text:
Now we’ve imported our data, the next thing to do is put it in a map and see what it looks like. This is really important - in many cases it is really easy to visually spot outliers or erroneous GPS fixes. To be honest, I also find it useful to use a GUI (graphical user interface) software like QGIS to visualise GPS tracking data, since you can then click on each GPS point and get information immediately. In R, this can probably be done too, but might be a bit slower/clunkier.

Very basic maps - movement over time

# basic map using the plot function
# colouring the number of rows instead of time
plot(
  duck1_y2$longitude,
  duck1_y2$latitude,
  col = viridis_pal()(nrow(duck1_y2)),
  pch = 20,
  xlab = "x",
  ylab = "y"
)

# with colour by time
cols <- viridis_pal()(100)

time_scaled <- rescale(as.numeric(duck1_y2$time), to = c(1, 100))

plot(
  duck1_y2$longitude,
  duck1_y2$latitude,
  col = cols[round(time_scaled)],
  pch = 20,
  xlab = "Longitude",
  ylab = "Latitude"
)

This is a nice quick start, but we can make something prettier.


Preparing our map data
To make our map using the ggmap package, we first create a bounding box of our data. This is just the outer GPS coordinates, so we know we can view ALL our data in the map.

# Step 1: make a cool map showing locations of the duck over time

# first, make a bounding box
bbox_duck1_y2 <- ggmap::make_bbox(
  lon = duck1_y2$longitude,
  lat = duck1_y2$latitude,
  f = 0.1
)

Next, we need to use a given R basemap to plot our tracking data onto. We will use stadiamaps. Go to their website to sign up and get your free API key, activate it (in the “First Steps in R” chapter) and then run this code below:

# load data from stadiamap
mybasemap_duck1_y2 <- get_stadiamap(bbox_duck1_y2, zoom = 12)

Since tracking data is a time-series trajectory, it is really useful to colour the tracks over time. To do this, we will set the start and end dates and points here.

# create a colour scale legend with start and end dates or remove the legend
start_date_duck1_y2 <- format(min(duck1_y2$time), "%Y-%m-%d")
end_date_duck1_y2 <- format(max(duck1_y2$time), "%Y-%m-%d")

# extract first and last points from dataset
start_point_duck1_y2 <- duck1_y2[1, ]
end_point_duck1_2 <- duck1_y2[nrow(duck1_y2), ]



Plotting our map using ggmap
The time has finally come! Are you ready to plot your own epic map? Give the code below a crack.

(mymap_paths_duck1_y2 <- ggmap(mybasemap_duck1_y2) +
  geom_point(
    data = duck1_y2,
    aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, colour = t)
  ) +
  geom_path(
    data = duck1_y2,
    aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, colour = t)
  ) +
  # add a title
  ggtitle("Duck 1 year 2 movement path") +

  # customise axis labels and colour scale
  labs(x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
  scale_color_distiller(
    name = "time",
    palette = "YlOrBr",
    direction = 1,
    breaks = c(min(duck1_y2$t), max(duck1_y2$t)),
    labels = c(start_date_duck1_y2, end_date_duck1_y2)
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom"))

# check out the plot
mymap_paths_duck1_y2



Saving our map
It’s always important to save your plots in an appropriate folder. A folder, say, like the ones we set up in the First Steps section!

ggsave(
  filename = "03_plots/duck1_y2_movement_path.png",
  plot = mymap_paths_duck1_y2,
  width = 8,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)



Animating our map
Seeing all the tracking data in one static image is cool and all, but how about we breathe some life into our map? Thankfully, this is easy to do with the gganimate package. The keys are the transition_reveal() and anim_save() functions. Play with the number of frames and frames per second to alter the length of your gif. This will depend on the duration and resolution of your dataset, and the purpose of the gif.

# now to make it into a gif!
path_animate_plot_duck1_y2 <- mymap_paths_duck1_y2 +
  transition_reveal(along = time) +
  labs(
    title = "Duck 1 year 2 movement path",
    subtitle = 'Date: {format(frame_along, "%Y-%m-%d")}'
  )

# animate and save
anim_save(
  filename = "03_plots/duck1_y2_movement_path.gif",
  animation = animate(path_animate_plot_duck1_y2, nframes = 100, fps = 10)
)

Now, open your gif file up in a browser. Well done! You should have a fully-fledged gif. Wowzers!

title: Revisitation analysis using the recurse package
text:
The recurse package is a simple but very effective tool. Other movement ecology analyses like kernel density estimates look at an animal’s overall intensity of space use, but they don’t take into account revisitations. Some places animals revisit are really important; their dens, feeding sites and water sources, for example. It also ties into human-wildlife relations; how often does an animal visit settlement boundaries, a road, a farm? Recurse offers an easy way to find these things out.
Vignette (2024): https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/recurse/vignettes/recurse.html
Recurse accepts two formats of data: 1) a simple 4-column dataframe: x y t id
x : x coords y: y coords t: datetime id: id name e.g. duck1
Note: x and y coordinates must NOT be latlon decimal degrees, but a use projection in meters Recurse can also work with move objects (from the move original package, not move2)
In this example, we will work with the dataframe example.
I am first transforming the coordinate columns of my duck1_y2 move2 object from WGS84 (a decimal degrees projection) to EPSG 7855 (a meters-based projection suitable for Australia) using the st_transform() function from the sf package. Then, I extract the xy coordinates using sf::st_coordinates() and assemble my dataframe.

# The recurse package supports both move objects and data frames
# here we demonstrate creating a data frame with the x, y, time, and id
# duck1_y2.df = as.data.frame
# convert duck1_y2_mv into projected coord system in m (WGS84 is lat long, not suitable for distance-based analysis)

# using EPSG 7855
duck1_y2_mv_7855 <- sf::st_transform(duck1_y2_mv, crs = 7855)
# now make recurse input dataframe
duck1_y2.df = data.frame(st_coordinates(duck1_y2_mv_7855))
duck1_y2.df$time = duck1_y2_mv_7855$time
duck1_y2.df$id = "duck1_y2"


Deciding patch size
The main criteria for deciding patch size is what your question is. Are you looking at large-scale foraging movements (in which case you want a larger patch size), or small-scale denning revisitations (in which case a smaller patch size is more suitable).
If you are unsure how to choose, the recurse vignette shares how to test different radii. https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/recurse/vignettes/recurse.html

# information to select radius
# calculate time and distance of each step
timeDiff = diff(as.numeric(duck1_y2.df$time) / 3600) # in hours
distDiff = sqrt(diff(duck1_y2.df$X)^2 + diff(duck1_y2.df$Y)^2)

sum(timeDiff > 1) / length(timeDiff)
# 0.5088308

# make a histogram
hist(
  distDiff,
  breaks = 30,
  xlab = "Step Length",
  main = "Duck 1 year 2 Step Length - frequency",
  col = "gray70"
)
# We can see there's probably an outlier since our line goes all the way to 10,000.



Running a basic recurse analysis
Let’s say we’ve decided on a 50m patch radius, since we want to understand relatively small-scale patch revisitation (e.g. nesting). We simply run getRecursions() on our data and specify the radius size.
The recurse objecct has various aspects, as shown below. Have a look and see what they are like.

# 500m radius as neighbourhood movement analysis
duck1_y2visit50 = getRecursions(duck1_y2.df, 50)

# different aspects of recurse object
duck1_y2visit50$revisits
duck1_y2visit50$residenceTime
duck1_y2visit50$radius
duck1_y2visit50$dists
duck1_y2visit50$revisitStats
duck1_y2visit50$timeunits


# plot results
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), las = 1, bty = "l")
plot(duck1_y2visit50, duck1_y2.df) # full view
drawCircle(275000, 5763000, 500) # shows what 50m radius looks like
plot(
  duck1_y2visit50,
  duck1_y2.df,
  xlim = c(280000, 285000),
  ylim = c(5762000, 5769000)
) # zoomed in

hist(
  duck1_y2visit50$revisits,
  breaks = 20,
  xlab = "Revisitations",
  main = "Duck 1 year 2 50m revisits - frequency",
  col = "gray70"
)
hist(
  duck1_y2visit50$revisitStats$timeInside,
  breaks = 20,
  xlab = "Time inside (h)",
  main = "Duck 1 year 2 50m revisits - time inside",
  col = "gray70"
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

There are many things we can do with this data. For example, additional metrics can be examined on a per visit basis.
For example, one could examine the correlation of visit length with visit entrance time.

# If needed, ensure `entranceTime` is in POSIXct format
# duck1_y2visit50$revisitStats$entranceTime <- as.POSIXct(duck1_y2visit50$revisitStats$entranceTime, format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")

# Extract the hour from `entranceTime`
duck1_y2visit50$revisitStats <- duck1_y2visit50$revisitStats %>%
  mutate(entranceHour = format(entranceTime, "%H")) # Extract hour as a factor

# Create the boxplot
ggplot(duck1_y2visit50$revisitStats, aes(x = entranceHour, y = timeInside)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Entrance Hour (Hour of Day)",
    y = "Visit Duration (h)",
    title = "Duck 1 50m Patch Visit Duration by Entrance Hour"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

Recurse offers various other ways to look at revisitations: - Revisits to a given polygon (e.g. a national park boundary, farm field, town boundaries) - Revisits to specified locations (we can set ourselves) - Revisits to clustered locations (e.g. systematically identifying heavily-visited areas (i.e. in the top 20% of revisited sites) using k-means clustering)
For all options, revisitation analyses can be done on multiple individuals, not just individual trajectories. E.g. if we want to understand the commonly re-visited areas, this is perfect.
To learn more, use the updated 2024 recurse vignette here: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/recurse/vignettes/recurse.html

title: First Steps in R
text:
Introduction
In this tutorial, we will install and load the packages required for the Movement Ecology Toolbox. We will also set up a convenient folder structure for organising our R projects and data management.


Install packages

install.packages("pak")
pak::pkg_install("usethis")
pak::pkg_install("tidyverse")
pak::pkg_install("devtools")
pak::pkg_install("dygraphs")
pak::pkg_install("ggmap")
pak::pkg_install("gganimate")
pak::pkg_install("geosphere")
pak::pkg_install("move2")
pak::pkg_install("sf")
pak::pkg_install("units")
pak::pkg_install("recurse")
pak::pkg_install("ctmm")
pak::pkg_install("amt")
pak::pkg_install("terra")
pak::pkg_install("fields")



Load packages

library(usethis)
library(tidyverse)
library(devtools)
library(dygraphs)
library(ggmap)
library(gganimate)
library(geosphere)
library(move2)
library(sf)
library(units)
library(recurse)
library(ctmm)
library(amt)
library(terra)
library(fields)



Additional settings for good data science
Set R so it doesn’t save any data in the environment/variables section between sessions. It might be annoying at first, but it is great practice to ensure you write every R script in a way that it loads all the variables you need. This makes it much easier when sharing your R projects with others, or if you return to your project after a while and forget how to load the objects you need!

usethis::use_blank_slate()

I also really recommend using the r4np (R for non-programmers) function here to set up convenient folders for organisation and data management. Within your working directory, it will create separate folders for: - raw data - tidy data - R scripts - plot - reports - miscellaneous

pak::pkg_install("ddauber/r4np")
library(r4np)
r4np::create_project_folder()



Working directories
We need to check our working directory and set it to the correct location. This way, we can use relative file paths to load and save data, which is more efficient and less error-prone than using absolute file paths.

getwd()
# all good
# if not, set to:
setwd(
  "/Users/jamiebolam/Documents/Conservation & Career/Career/DPhil/Deakin x Druid GPS trackers/PhD/Coding Club/Jamie - Movement Ecology Toolbox/move_ecol_coding_club_deakin"
)
# or your own working directory
# then check it worked
getwd()



Additional settings for ggmaps:
For ggmaps: get a stadiamap API key

ggmap::register_stadiamaps(
  key = "inset-your-stadiamaps-api-key-here",
  write = TRUE
)
